summary.text: Using $24p(t)+1=(6t+1)^2$, the proof reduces the construction to quadratic forms: Dirichlet’s theorem and reduction of positive-definite ternary forms of determinant $2$ show that every $K\equiv13\pmod{24}$ has an odd representation by $3x^2+4y^2+6z^2$, with a $3$-adic descent supplying the required form. For large $n$, two suitable parameters in the same residue class modulo $9$, chosen near $\sqrt{(24n+7)/16}$, turn these representations into two distinct positive quadruples congruent to $1\pmod6$; finite enumeration through $214000$ supplies two representations off the exceptional set and counts the exceptional cases exactly.

full_proof.text:
Put
\[
p(t)=\frac{t(3t+1)}2\qquad(t\in\mathbb N),
\]
and let \(S(n)\) be the set of quadruples \((x,y,z,w)\in\mathbb N^4\) such that
\[
x\le y,
\qquad n=p(x)+p(y)+2p(z)+3p(w).
\tag{1}
\]
Thus \(a(n)=|S(n)|\). We prove that all \(n>5\) have a representation and that the only values represented exactly once are
\[
E=\{0,2,7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41\}.
\]
In fact, except for the elements of \(E\) and the zero values \(1,3,5\), we prove the stronger inequality \(a(n)\ge2\).

First note the elementary bounds
\[
t\le p(t),\qquad p(j)\le p(k)\quad(0\le j\le k).
\tag{2}
\]
Consequently every coordinate occurring in (1) is at most \(n\), so counting quadruples in \(\{0,\ldots,n\}^4\) counts all representations. More generally, if \(n<p(B)\), then every coordinate in a representation is less than \(B\); hence in this case \(a(n)\) can be computed by searching only \(0\le x,y,z,w<B\).

We first establish the number-theoretic result used for all sufficiently large \(n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Two facts about integral quadratic forms
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Write an integral ternary quadratic form as
\[
F(x,y,z)=ax^2+by^2+cz^2+2pxy+2qxz+2ryz,
\]
with determinant
\[
\Delta(F)=abc+2pqr-ar^2-bq^2-cp^2.
\]
The form is positive definite if \(F(x,y,z)>0\) for every nonzero integral triple.

We need the following result.

**Lemma 1.** If \(F\) is a positive definite integral ternary form and
\[
0<\Delta(F)\le2,
\]
then every integer represented by \(F\) is represented by
\[
X^2+Y^2+\Delta(F)Z^2.
\tag{3}
\]

We give the proof, including the reduction estimate.

For a positive definite binary form
\[
G(y,z)=Ay^2+2Byz+Cz^2,
\qquad A>0,
\qquad AC-B^2>0,
\]
choose a nonzero integral pair \((y_0,z_0)\) on which \(G\) has its least positive value \(\mu\). This pair is primitive: if a common divisor \(g\ge2\) divided both coordinates, division by \(g\) would give a nonzero pair with value \(\mu/g^2<\mu\).

Complete \((y_0,z_0)\) to a unimodular basis. Thus choose integers \(s,t\) with
\[
y_0s+z_0t=1,
\]
and use the substitution
\[
y=y_0Y-tZ,\qquad z=z_0Y+sZ.
\]
It transforms \(G\) into
\[
\mu Y^2+2B'YZ+C'Z^2,
\qquad \mu C'-B'^2=AC-B^2.
\tag{4}
\]
Choose an integer \(Y\) nearest to \(-B'/\mu\), in the precise form
\[
|2(\mu Y+B')|\le\mu.
\tag{5}
\]
The vector corresponding to \((Y,1)\) is nonzero, so minimality of \(\mu\), together with
\[
4\mu(\mu Y^2+2B'Y+C')
  =[2(\mu Y+B')]^2+4(\mu C'-B'^2),
\]
gives
\[
4\mu^2\le \mu^2+4(AC-B^2).
\]
Therefore
\[
3\mu^2\le4(AC-B^2).
\tag{6}
\]
This is the binary Hermite estimate needed below.

Now let \(m\) be the least positive value of the ternary form \(F\). A vector attaining \(m\) is primitive by the same division argument. Every primitive vector in \(\mathbb Z^3\) extends to a unimodular integral basis: this follows by two applications of Bezout's identity, or equivalently by constructing two further columns whose determinant with the given vector is \(1\). After this unimodular change of variables, the new form, still denoted by \(F\), has first coefficient \(a=m\), has the same determinant, and all its nonzero values are at least \(m\).

The Schur-complement identity is
\[
mF(x,y,z)=(mx+py+qz)^2+G(y,z),
\tag{7}
\]
where
\[
G(y,z)=(mb-p^2)y^2+2(mr-pq)yz+(mc-q^2)z^2.
\]
Positive definiteness shows that its first coefficient is positive, and direct expansion gives
\[
\det G=m\Delta(F).
\tag{8}
\]
Apply (6) to \(G\), obtaining a nonzero pair \((y,z)\) with value, say, \(g>0\), satisfying
\[
3g^2\le4m\Delta(F)\le8m.
\tag{9}
\]
Choose \(x\) so that
\[
|2(mx+py+qz)|\le m.
\tag{10}
\]
Since \((x,y,z)\ne(0,0,0)\), minimality and (7) imply
\[
m^2\le(mx+py+qz)^2+g\le \frac{m^2}{4}+g.
\]
Thus \(3m^2\le4g\). Squaring this and using (9) gives
\[
27m^4\le128m,
\qquad\text{hence}\qquad 27m^3\le128.
\]
A positive integer \(m\ge2\) would violate the last inequality. Therefore \(m=1\): every such ternary form represents \(1\).

Again put a primitive vector representing \(1\) first in a unimodular basis. The form now has first coefficient \(1\), and (7) becomes
\[
F(x,y,z)=(x+py+qz)^2+G(y,z),
\tag{11}
\]
where \(G\) is a positive binary integral form of determinant \(\Delta(F)\). By (6), \(G\) represents a positive integer \(g\) with
\[
3g^2\le4\Delta(F)\le8.
\]
Thus \(g=1\). Put a primitive vector representing \(1\) first in a unimodular basis for this binary form. It takes the shape
\[
Y^2+2B'YZ+C'Z^2=(Y+B'Z)^2+(C'-B'^2)Z^2,
\]
and its determinant says \(C'-B'^2=\Delta(F)\). Combining this with (11), and undoing the unimodular coordinate changes, proves (3), and hence Lemma 1.

We will also use the familiar positive-definiteness criterion implicit above. Namely, if
\[
a>0,\qquad ab-p^2>0,
\qquad \Delta(F)>0,
\tag{12}
\]
then \(F\) is positive definite. It follows from the identity
\[
a(ab-p^2)F(x,y,z)
=(ab-p^2)(ax+py+qz)^2
+\bigl((ab-p^2)y+(ar-pq)z\bigr)^2
+a\Delta(F)z^2.
\tag{13}
\]
If \((x,y,z)\ne0\), the right side cannot vanish under (12).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Representing numbers congruent to 5 modulo 8
--------------------------------------------------------------------

**Lemma 2.** If \(K\in\mathbb N\) and \(K\equiv5\pmod8\), then
\[
K=X^2+Y^2+2Z^2
\tag{14}
\]
for some integers \(X,Y,Z\).

Choose, by Dirichlet's theorem on primes in arithmetic progressions, a prime \(P>8K\) such that
\[
P\equiv4K-1\pmod{8K}.
\tag{15}
\]
The residue \(4K-1\) is coprime to \(8K\): any common divisor divides both \(4K-1\) and \(2(4K)-2(4K-1)=2\), while \(4K-1\) is odd. From (15),
\[
P\equiv3\pmod8,
\qquad K\mid P+1.
\tag{16}
\]
We claim that \(-2K\) is a quadratic residue modulo \(P\). Indeed,
\[
\left(\frac{-2K}{P}\right)
=\left(\frac{-2}{P}\right)\left(\frac K P\right).
\]
For \(P\equiv3\pmod8\), \(\left(\frac{-2}{P}\right)=1\). Also \(K\equiv1\pmod4\), so quadratic reciprocity for the Jacobi symbol gives
\[
\left(\frac K P\right)=\left(\frac P K\right)
 =\left(\frac{-1}K\right)=1,
\]
because \(P\equiv-1\pmod K\) and \(K\equiv1\pmod4\). This proves the claim.

Choose \(s\) modulo \(P\) with \(s^2\equiv-2K\pmod P\). Since \(P>K>0\), \(K\) is invertible modulo \(P\). Put \(e\equiv sK^{-1}\pmod P\). Then
\[
Ke^2\equiv-2\pmod P.
\]
Take a nonnegative representative \(e_0\), and define positive integers
\[
b=\frac{P+1}{K},
\qquad c=\frac{2+Ke_0^2}{P}.
\]
Consider
\[
F(x,y,z)=Kx^2+by^2+cz^2+2xy+2e_0yz.
\]
Its determinant is
\[
Kbc-Ke_0^2-c=c(Kb-1)-Ke_0^2=cP-Ke_0^2=2.
\]
Moreover, its leading coefficient is \(K>0\), its leading \(2\times2\) minor is
\[
Kb-1=P>0,
\]
and its determinant is positive. Thus (13) shows that \(F\) is positive definite. Lemma 1, applied to the value \(F(1,0,0)=K\), yields (14).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. A representation adapted to congruences modulo 6
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next prove the crucial refinement.

**Lemma 3.** If \(K\equiv13\pmod{24}\), then there are odd integers \(T,y,E\) such that
\[
K=3T^2+4y^2+6E^2.
\tag{17}
\]

By Lemma 2, write
\[
K=X^2+Y^2+2Z^2.
\tag{18}
\]
Since \(K\equiv1\pmod3\), a check of the three square residues modulo \(3\) gives one of
\[
3\mid X-Z,
\qquad 3\mid X+Z,
\qquad 3\mid Y\text{ and }3\mid Z.
\tag{19}
\]
We use (19) in a descent. Suppose first that \(Y\) is even, say \(Y=2y\). If \(X=3d+Z\), then direct expansion gives
\[
X^2+Y^2+2Z^2=3(d+Z)^2+4y^2+6d^2.
\tag{20}
\]
If \(X=3d-Z\), similarly
\[
X^2+Y^2+2Z^2=3(d-Z)^2+4y^2+6d^2.
\tag{21}
\]
These are already of the required shape.

It remains to handle the third alternative in (19). Write \(Y=3Y_1\), \(Z=3Z_1\). The two identities
\[
(3Y_1)^2+2(3Z_1)^2
 =(Y_1+4Z_1)^2+2(2Y_1-Z_1)^2
\tag{22}
\]
and
\[
(3Y_1)^2+2(3Z_1)^2
 =(Y_1-4Z_1)^2+2(-2Y_1-Z_1)^2
\tag{23}
\]
produce new representations of the same shape as (18), with the first coordinate still \(X\). Since \(Y\) is even and \(3\) is odd, \(Y_1\), and hence both new middle coordinates, are even.

This descent cannot continue indefinitely. More explicitly, fix an exponent \(j\) such that \(3^j\) does not divide both the current second and third coordinates. If both pairs on the right sides of (22) and (23) were divisible by \(3^{j-1}\), then adding and subtracting their coordinates, and using that \(2\) and \(4\) are coprime to \(3^j\), would imply that \(3^{j-1}\) divides both \(Y_1,Z_1\). It would follow that \(3^j\) divides the original \(Y,Z\), a contradiction. Thus one transformation lowers the exponent.

Such a starting exponent always exists when \((Y,Z)\ne(0,0)\); for example \(j=|Y|+|Z|\) works, since \(3^j>|Y|+|Z|\), so a nonzero one of \(Y,Z\) cannot be divisible by \(3^j\). Thus induction on \(j\) eventually reaches (20) or (21), proving a representation
\[
K=3x^2+4y^2+6z^2.
\tag{24}
\]

For completeness, the parity needed to begin the descent is automatic after possibly interchanging \(X\) and \(Y\). Squares modulo \(8\) are \(0,1,4\). Since \(K\equiv5\pmod8\), if \(X\) is odd then \(Y\) is even; otherwise use \(Y\) as the first coordinate and the even \(X\) as the second. The relevant second and third coordinates cannot both be zero, as that would make a square congruent to \(13\pmod{24}\), which is impossible. Finally, reducing (24) modulo \(8\) shows that all three of \(x,y,z\) are odd: checking square residues \(0,1,4\) in
\[
3x^2+4y^2+6z^2\equiv5\pmod8
\]
forces each square to be odd. This proves Lemma 3.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. The explicit design producing a pentagonal representation
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Use the identity
\[
24p(t)+1=(6t+1)^2.
\tag{25}
\]
It follows that if positive integers \(v_1,v_2,v_3,v_4\), all congruent to \(1\pmod6\), satisfy
\[
v_1^2+v_2^2+2v_3^2+3v_4^2=24n+7,
\tag{26}
\]
then writing \(v_i=6t_i+1\) and using (25) gives
\[
n=p(t_1)+p(t_2)+2p(t_3)+3p(t_4).
\]
Interchanging \(v_1,v_2\) if necessary enforces \(t_1\le t_2\).

We now construct such \(v_i\). Put
\[
N=24n+7.
\]
Suppose an integer \(m\) satisfies
\[
m\ge0,
\qquad m\equiv1\pmod3,
\qquad N-16m^2\equiv39\pmod{72},
\tag{27}
\]
and
\[
16m^2<N,
\qquad 15N<256m^2.
\tag{28}
\]
Then
\[
K=\frac{N-16m^2}{3}
\]
is a positive integer, and (27) gives \(K\equiv13\pmod{24}\). By Lemma 3, choose odd \(T_0,y_0,E\) with
\[
K=3T_0^2+4y_0^2+6E^2.
\tag{29}
\]
A square-residue check modulo \(3\) in (29), using \(K\equiv1\pmod3\), shows that \(3\nmid y_0\). Replace \(y_0\) by one of its two signs so that
\[
y\equiv5\pmod6,
\qquad y^2=y_0^2.
\tag{30}
\]
Since \(T_0,y\) are odd, write \(T_0=y+2g\). Replace \(T_0\) by its negative if necessary. Of the two resulting values of \((T-y)/2\), exactly one makes
\[
m+\frac{T-y}{2}\equiv1\pmod2.
\]
Write
\[
T=y+2g',
\qquad m+g'\equiv1\pmod2.
\tag{31}
\]
Now define
\[
\begin{aligned}
v_1&=m+3E-3y-3g',\\
v_2&=m-3E-3y-3g',\\
v_3&=m+3g',\\
v_4&=2m+y.
\end{aligned}
\tag{32}
\]
Substituting (29), with \(T=y+2g'\), gives the exact identity
\[
v_1^2+v_2^2+2v_3^2+3v_4^2
 =16m^2+3K=N.
\tag{33}
\]

We check positivity, which is the reason for the second inequality in (28). Since \(N=16m^2+3K\), that inequality is equivalent to
\[
45K<16m^2.
\tag{34}
\]
The following identities are direct expansions using (29):
\[
\begin{aligned}
7\bigl(45K-16(3E-3y-3g')^2\bigr)
 &=18(7E+8(y+g'))^2+45(6(y+g')-7y)^2,\\
7\bigl(45K-16(-3E-3y-3g')^2\bigr)
 &=18(-7E+8(y+g'))^2+45(6(y+g')-7y)^2,\\
21K-16(3g')^2
 &=3(6(y+g')+y)^2+126E^2,\\
K-4y^2&=3(y+2g')^2+6E^2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{35}
\]
The right sides are nonnegative. If \(v_1\le0\), then from its definition and \(m\ge0\),
\[
m^2\le(-3E+3y+3g')^2,
\]
whereas the first identity in (35) and (34) give the strict reverse inequality. Thus \(v_1>0\). The second identity similarly gives \(v_2>0\). The third identity, together with (34), shows \((3g')^2<m^2\), contradicting \(v_3\le0\); hence \(v_3>0\). Finally, if \(v_4=2m+y\le0\), then \(y^2\ge4m^2\), while the last identity gives \(K\ge4y^2\ge16m^2\), again contradicting (34). Thus all four coordinates are positive.

The congruences in (27), (30), and (31), together with the oddness of \(E\), give directly
\[
v_1\equiv v_2\equiv v_3\equiv v_4\equiv1\pmod6.
\tag{36}
\]
For example, modulo \(3\) this follows from \(m\equiv1\), except for \(v_4\), where \(2m+y\equiv2+2\equiv1\); modulo \(2\), (31), (30), and the oddness of \(E\) make every expression in (32) odd. Therefore (25), (33), and (36) produce a member \((x,y,z,w)\in S(n)\).

This construction also records the linear invariant
\[
(6x+1)+(6y+1)+2(6z+1)+6(6w+1)=16m.
\tag{37}
\]
Indeed, the left side is \(v_1+v_2+2v_3+6v_4\), independent of whether \(v_1,v_2\) were interchanged, and (32) reduces it to \(16m\). Thus constructions arising from distinct values of \(m\) give distinct representations.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Two representations for every \(n\ge214001\)
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(n\ge214001\), let \(N=24n+7\), and put
\[
s=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{24n+6}{16}}\right\rfloor.
\]
Then
\[
16s^2\le24n+6<16(s+1)^2,
\qquad s\ge566.
\tag{38}
\]
According to the residue of \(n\) modulo \(3\), choose
\[
r=\begin{cases}
4,&n\equiv0\pmod3,\\
7,&n\equiv1\pmod3,\\
1,&n\equiv2\pmod3.
\end{cases}
\tag{39}
\]
In every case \(0\le r<9\), \(r\equiv1\pmod3\), and direct reduction modulo \(72\) gives
\[
N-16r^2\equiv39\pmod{72}.
\tag{40}
\]
Let \(m_2\) be the largest integer at most \(s\) congruent to \(r\pmod9\), and put
\[
m_1=m_2-9.
\]
Then
\[
s-8\le m_2\le s,

theoremqquad s-17\le m_1<m_2,
\tag{41}
\]
and \(m_1,m_2\ge0\) because \(s\ge566\). Both are congruent to \(r\pmod9\), so both are \(1\pmod3\). Moreover, \(m_i^2\equiv r^2\pmod9\); multiplying by \(16\) shows from (40) that
\[
N-16m_i^2\equiv39\pmod{72}.
\tag{42}
\]
The upper bounds \(m_i\le s\) and (38) imply
\[
16m_i^2<N.
\tag{43}
\]
For the lower inequality, (38), (41), and \(s\ge566\) give
\[
15N<256(s-17)^2\le256m_i^2.
\tag{44}
\]
This is an elementary expansion: use \(N<16(s+1)^2+1\), and check
\[
15\bigl(16(s+1)^2+1\bigr)<256(s-17)^2
\]
for \(s\ge566\); after expansion the difference is increasing and already positive at \(566\).

Thus both \(m_1\) and \(m_2\) satisfy (27) and (28). The design above supplies two representations in \(S(n)\). They are distinct by (37), because \(m_1\ne m_2\). Therefore
\[
a(n)\ge2\qquad(n\ge214001).
\tag{45}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The finite range
--------------------------------------------------------------------

It remains to handle \(n\le214000\). This is done by a finite avoidance computation whose precise mathematical content is as follows.

Encode a quadruple \((x,y,z,w)\), with each coordinate below \(512\), by
\[
e=x+512y+512^2z+512^3w.
\tag{46}
\]
Decoding by successive quotient and remainder operations recovers the four coordinates uniquely. A certificate for a fixed \(n\) consists of two encoded integers \(e_1<e_2\). It is accepted exactly when both decoded quadruples satisfy \(x\le y\) and equation (1). Because decoding is injective, \(e_1<e_2\) proves that the two representations are distinct, and hence proves \(a(n)\ge2\).

Pairs of such certificates were packed consecutively, one pair for each integer in an interval. Direct decoding and evaluation of \(p(x)+p(y)+2p(z)+3p(w)\) established certificates on the following intervals:
\[
\begin{gathered}
\{4\},\ \{6\},\ \{8\},\ \{10\},\ [13,15],\ [17,30],\ \{32\},\ [34,40],\\
[42,20041],\ [20042,40041],\ [40042,60041],\ [60042,80041],\\
[80042,100041],\ [100042,120041],\ [120042,140041],\\
[140042,160041],\ [160042,180041],\ [180042,200041],\ [200042,220041].
\end{gathered}
\tag{47}
\]
For the long intervals, the computation was organized into twenty blocks of one thousand consecutive values; for the short intervals it used the displayed interval length. Thus (47) covers every integer from \(4\) through \(214000\) except
\[
5,7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41.
\]
Accordingly,
\[
a(n)\ge2
\tag{48}
\]
for every \(4\le n\le214000\) outside that list. Notice that every encoded coordinate is below \(512\), but this does not restrict the conclusion: each decoded item is an actual representation, and two actual representations suffice for the lower bound.

The remaining exact small cardinalities were obtained by complete bounded enumeration. By (2), to count \(a(n)\) it is enough to search coordinates below any \(B\) with \(n<p(B)\). The enumeration gives
\[
\begin{array}{c|c|c}
n&a(n)&\text{the unique quadruple when }a(n)=1\\ \hline
0&1&(0,0,0,0)\\
1&0&\\
2&1&(0,1,0,0)\\
3&0&\\
5&0&\\
7&1&(0,2,0,0)\\
9&1&(1,2,0,0)\\
11&1&(0,2,1,0)\\
12&1&(0,1,1,1)\\
16&1&(0,1,2,0)\\
31&1&(1,3,2,0)\\
33&1&(2,4,0,0)\\
41&1&(3,4,0,0).
\end{array}
\tag{49}
\]
For instance, bounds \(B=1,2,3,4,5,6\), as appropriate, suffice respectively because
\[
p(1)=2,
p(2)=7,
p(3)=15,
p(4)=26,
p(5)=40,
p(6)=57.
\]
Searching all \(0\le x,y,z,w<B\), retaining only \(x\le y\) and equation (1), yields exactly the entries in (49). This is exhaustive by (2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Conclusion
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Combining (45), (48), and (49), every natural number other than
\[
0,1,2,3,5,7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41
\]
has at least two representations. The values \(1,3,5\) have none, and precisely the ten values in \(E\) have one.

If \(n>5\), then either \(n\in\{7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41\}\), in which case (49) gives one representation, or \(n\) is outside that set, in which case (45) or (48) gives at least two. Hence \(a(n)>0\) for every \(n>5\).

Finally, (49) proves \(a(n)=1\) for every \(n\in E\). Conversely, if \(a(n)=1\), then \(n\) cannot be \(1,3,5\), where the value is zero, and cannot be any other number, where the value is at least two. Therefore
\[
a(n)=1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{0,2,7,9,11,12,16,31,33,41\}.
\]
This proves both assertions.
